summary: ML-DSA is a post-quantum digital signature scheme defined by NIST in FIPS 204. This document specifies how to use it in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) for signing messages.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains how to put a signature that resists future quantum computers on signed messages and files.

questions: how to use ml-dsa in cms
which digest algorithm for ml-dsa cms
subtitle: How to sign CMS messages with ML-DSA, a signature scheme designed to resist quantum computers.

tldr.problem: ML-DSA is a post-quantum signature algorithm standardised by NIST in FIPS 204, but the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) needs to know exactly how to name it and how to feed it data.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns one algorithm identifier per parameter set (ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, ML-DSA-87), uses only the pure mode of ML-DSA, and says how the SignerInfo fields are filled in, with SHA-512 as the digest that MUST be supported.
tldr.outcome: CMS signed-data can carry ML-DSA signatures in an interoperable way. The RFC also warns that the private key must be protected and that good random numbers are essential.

today: RFC 9882 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) is a post-quantum signature algorithm standardised by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). It aims to stay secure against an adversary with a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer. The RFC says it offers smaller signatures and significantly faster runtimes than SLH-DSA, another NIST post-quantum signature algorithm.

This document specifies ML-DSA in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) at three security levels: ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87. Before standardisation ML-DSA was known as Dilithium, and the two are not compatible. FIPS 204 also defines a pre-hashed variant called HashML-DSA, which this RFC does not specify for CMS.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a new kind of digital signature built to stay safe from future quantum computers. This document explains how to use it on signed messages, in three strengths.

sections.title: ML-DSA Algorithm Identifiers
sections.content:
CMS and X.509 name algorithms with an AlgorithmIdentifier. Each ML-DSA parameter set has its own object identifier, defined in the NIST Computer Security Objects Register: id-ml-dsa-44, id-ml-dsa-65 and id-ml-dsa-87. They are numbered 17, 18 and 19 under the NIST signature algorithm arc. The same identifiers name ML-DSA public keys and signature algorithms, and RFC 9881 covers their use in X.509 certificates.

Because the parameter set is already implied by the OID, the parameters field MUST be omitted when encoding an ML-DSA AlgorithmIdentifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Each of the three strengths gets its own name tag. The name tag already says everything, so there is no extra note to attach.

sections.title: Pure Mode, Not Pre-Hash Mode
sections.content:
CMS signatures were originally made over a digest computed outside the signature algorithm. Newer algorithms such as EdDSA, SLH-DSA and ML-DSA support a pure mode, where the message goes straight into the algorithm, and a pre-hash mode, where a separately computed digest goes in.

For EdDSA (RFC 8419) and SLH-DSA (RFC 9814) only the pure mode is specified for CMS, and this RFC follows that convention. The reason given is that CMS signatures are usually computed over a small set of signed attributes containing a hash of the content, so pre-hash would not shrink the data to be signed and offers no benefit.
sections.plainLanguage: You can hand the whole letter to the signer, or hand over a short summary of it. Since CMS usually signs a short summary-style note anyway, the extra summary step would not help, so only the whole-thing way is used.

sections.title: Generating and Verifying Signatures
sections.content:
Two methods from RFC 5652 apply, depending on whether signedAttrs is present in the SignerInfo. Without signed attributes, the ML-DSA signature is computed over the content of the signed-data (the eContent OCTET STRING value, without tag and length octets). With signed attributes, it is computed over the complete DER encoding of the SignedAttrs value, using the EXPLICIT SET OF tag rather than the IMPLICIT [0] tag.

Signed attributes must include at least a content-type attribute and a message-digest attribute. Using signed attributes is preferred, and it helps performance when the content is large. The ML-DSA context string is set to the empty string.
sections.plainLanguage: If there is a cover note with a summary, the signer signs the cover note. If not, the signer signs the whole letter. Using the cover note is better, especially for a very long letter.

sections.title: What Goes in the SignerInfo
sections.content:
The digestAlgorithm field names the hash used for the signed attributes. A digest offering λ bits of strength with at least 2 * λ bits of output matches a parameter set, and the overall strength is limited by the weaker of the digest and the ML-DSA parameter set. SHA-512 MUST be supported and suits every parameter set. SHAKE256 SHOULD be supported, since ML-DSA uses it internally; it produces 512 bits of output in CMS. In both cases the digest identifier's parameters MUST be omitted.

If no signed attributes are present the digest algorithm has no meaning, but implementations MUST still specify SHA-512 for interoperability, and receivers MUST ignore the field. The signatureAlgorithm field MUST hold one of the three ML-DSA OIDs with parameters absent, and signature holds the value produced by FIPS 204.
sections.plainLanguage: The signer says which summary-maker they used and which of the three signature strengths. Everyone must understand the SHA-512 summary-maker, so it is the safe choice.

sections.title: Security and Operational Notes
sections.content:
Security of the ML-DSA private key is critical: if it is compromised, an adversary can forge arbitrary signatures. ML-DSA also depends on high-quality random numbers. By default signing is "hedged", mixing fresh randomness with randomness stored in the private key. A deterministic variant is allowed and verifies the same way, but signers SHOULD NOT use it where side-channel or fault attacks are a concern. To prevent algorithm substitution attacks, the CMSAlgorithmProtection attribute from RFC 6211 SHOULD be included in signed attributes.

Operationally, including signed attributes lets a hardware security module receive only the small attribute set instead of the full content. The external calculation of the μ message representative from FIPS 204 is another way to avoid sending the whole message to a device.
sections.plainLanguage: Guard your secret signing key like a house key, because anyone with it can sign as you. The signer also needs truly random numbers, like fairly shuffled cards.
